children: A measure of Australian consumer sentiment fell sharply for a second month in October, a survey showed on Tuesday, as rising interest rates added to cost of living pressures and squeezed family finances.

A Westpac-Melbourne Institute survey showed its main index of consumer sentiment slid 4.7% to 80.4 in October, adding to a 5.2% drop the previous month. The index was down almost 13% from a year earlier, with pessimists outnumbering optimists by a wide margin.

"At just over 80, the latest sentiment Index is amongst the forty worst reads since our monthly survey began in the early 1970s," said Matthew Hassan, Westpac's head of Australian macro-forecasting. "This marks the worst period of recurring extremely weak sentiment since the disastrous recession in the early 1990s."

The survey was taken as the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates for a fourth time this year, taking them to a 15-year high of 4.60%, and cautioned it might have to tighten further to curb inflation.
Hassan noted the 40% of responses taken after the RBA hike showed a confidence reading of just 67.2, compared to 86.9 for the 60% that preceded the RBA meeting.
The impact was clear in the survey's measure of family finances compared to a year ago which dived 8.0%, while the outlook for finances fell 6.4%.
A measure of the economic outlook also showed large declines, while the index on whether it was a good time to buy a major household item slid 7.1%.

title: Australia consumer sentiment slides in October as rates rise
